blocks.body:
Dirichlet proved that every progression $a,a+q,a+2q,\dots$ with $\gcd(a,q)=1$ contains infinitely many primes, and the prime number theorem for progressions says they are shared out equally: each of the $\varphi(q)$ admissible classes gets asymptotically $1/\varphi(q)$ of the primes. How fast does this equal sharing set in, and how large may $q$ be compared with $x$? The answer is controlled by the zeros of Dirichlet $L$-functions, just as the error in the prime number theorem is controlled by the zeros of $\zeta$.

The generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH) asserts that all these zeros lie on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=\tfrac12$. It contains the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]] as a special case and is open as of October 2026. Its consequences reach from primes in progressions to the running time of algorithms, which is why so many results in number theory and computer science are stated "under GRH".

blocks.title: Dirichlet L-functions and their zeros
blocks.body:
From [[dirichlet-characters]] and [[l-functions]]: a Dirichlet character $\chi$ modulo $q$ gives, for $\operatorname{Re}s>1,$

$$L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}=\prod_p\big(1-\chi(p)p^{-s}\big)^{-1}.$$

For the principal character $\chi_0$ modulo $q$, $L(s,\chi_0)=\zeta(s)\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-s})$, so its zeros in the strip are those of $\zeta$. For nonprincipal $\chi$, $L(s,\chi)$ is entire. If $\chi$ is primitive and nonprincipal, a functional equation relates $L(s,\chi)$ to $L(1-s,\bar\chi)$; it produces trivial zeros at $s=0,-2,-4,\dots$ when $\chi(-1)=1$ and at $s=-1,-3,-5,\dots$ when $\chi(-1)=-1$, and confines all other zeros, the nontrivial ones, to the critical strip $0< \operatorname{Re}s<1$. They are symmetric under $\rho\mapsto1-\bar\rho$ (the reflection in the critical line), but for complex $\chi$ not under $\rho\mapsto\bar\rho$ alone, since $\overline{L(\bar s,\chi)}=L(s,\bar\chi)$ swaps $\chi$ with $\bar\chi$.

Every character is induced by a primitive character $\chi^*$ of some conductor $q^*\mid q$, and

$$L(s,\chi)=L(s,\chi^*)\prod_{p\mid q}\big(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s}\big).$$

The finite product only adds zeros on the line $\operatorname{Re}s=0$ (see the first example below), so it is enough to state GRH for primitive characters.

blocks.title: The generalized Riemann hypothesis (conjecture)
blocks.body:
For every Dirichlet character $\chi$, every zero of $L(s,\chi)$ in the critical strip lies on the critical line:

$$L(\rho,\chi)=0,\ 0< \operatorname{Re}\rho<1\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Re}\rho=\tfrac12.$$

This is a conjecture, open as of October 2026. For $\chi$ principal it is the Riemann hypothesis.

blocks.title: A note on names
blocks.body: Naming varies. Some authors call the statement for Dirichlet $L$-functions the extended Riemann hypothesis and reserve "generalized" for larger families: the Dedekind zeta functions of number fields ([[dedekind-zeta]]), [[hecke-l|Hecke L-functions]], and beyond them automorphic $L$-functions. Some applications below need these stronger forms; we say so when they do.

blocks.title: Primes in progressions
blocks.body:
Let $\psi(x;q,a)=\sum_{n\le x,\ n\equiv a\ (q)}\Lambda(n)$. Orthogonality of characters picks out the class of $a$:

$$\psi(x;q,a)=\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}\bar\chi(a)\,\psi(x,\chi),\qquad\psi(x,\chi)=\sum_{n\le x}\chi(n)\Lambda(n).$$

The principal character contributes $\psi(x,\chi_0)/\varphi(q)$, which is $x/\varphi(q)$ plus the error from $\zeta$. Each other character contributes an error governed, through its explicit formula $\psi(x,\chi)\approx-\sum_\rho x^\rho/\rho$, by the zeros of $L(s,\chi)$. Under GRH every $|x^\rho|$ equals $\sqrt x$, and a careful truncation gives $\psi(x,\chi)=O(\sqrt x\log^2(qx))$ for nonprincipal $\chi$. This yields the main consequence.

blocks.title: Primes in progressions under GRH
blocks.body:
Assume GRH. Then for $x\ge2$, $1\le q\le x$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$,

$$\psi(x;q,a)=\frac x{\varphi(q)}+O\big(\sqrt x\log^2x\big),$$

with an absolute implied constant.

blocks.title: Reading the theorem
blocks.body:
The proof (omitted; see Davenport) is the truncated explicit formula for each $\psi(x,\chi)$, followed by the averaging above; the second example below carries out the averaging step. Note what the theorem says and does not say. The main term $x/\varphi(q)$ exceeds the error only when $\varphi(q)$ is smaller than about $\sqrt x/\log^2x$, so even GRH gives equidistribution only for moduli up to roughly $\sqrt x$.

Unconditionally, the [[siegel-walfisz|Siegel–Walfisz theorem]] gives an asymptotic only for $q\le(\log x)^A$, with an error term of the form $x\exp(-c\sqrt{\log x})$ and an ineffective constant. The gap between $(\log x)^A$ and $\sqrt x$ is enormous. It is partly closed, on average over $q$, by the following theorem.

blocks.title: Bombieri–Vinogradov (1965)
blocks.body:
For every $A>0$ there is $B=B(A)>0$ such that, with $Q=\sqrt x\,(\log x)^{-B}$,

$$\sum_{q\le Q}\ \max_{\gcd(a,q)=1}\left|\psi(x;q,a)-\frac x{\varphi(q)}\right|\ \ll_A\ \frac x{(\log x)^A}.$$

blocks.title: GRH on average
blocks.body:
Compare with GRH: GRH bounds each term by $O(\sqrt x\log^2x)$, so the sum over $q\le Q$ is $O(Q\sqrt x\log^2x)=O\big(x(\log x)^{2-B}\big)$. Bombieri–Vinogradov proves an estimate of the same strength unconditionally, provided one averages over the modulus. This is the precise meaning of the slogan that Bombieri–Vinogradov is GRH on average. Its proof uses the [[large-sieve]] in place of information about individual zeros; see [[bombieri-vinogradov]].

Going beyond $\sqrt x$ is a different matter. The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture asserts the same average bound with $Q=x^\theta$ for every $\theta<1$; it does not follow from GRH. Goldston, Pintz and Yıldırım showed that any level $\theta>\tfrac12$ would give bounded gaps between primes, a result later obtained unconditionally by Zhang and Maynard (see [[bounded-gaps]]).

blocks.title: Consequences for small numbers and algorithms
blocks.body:
Many algorithms need a small number with a given property, and GRH guarantees one exists.

- Least quadratic non-residue. Under GRH the least quadratic non-residue $n(p)$ modulo a prime $p$ is $O(\log^2p)$ (Ankeny, 1952), and explicitly $n(p)<2\log^2p$ (Bach, 1990). Unconditionally the best bound is Burgess's $n(p)\ll_\varepsilon p^{1/(4\sqrt e)+\varepsilon}$. Finding a non-residue is the one step of the Tonelli–Shanks square-root algorithm that is not known to be deterministic; under GRH it is.
- Primality. Under GRH every odd composite $n$ has a Miller–Rabin witness below $2\log^2n$ (Bach, sharpening Miller's 1976 result), so the Miller–Rabin test becomes deterministic polynomial-time; see [[primality]]. Since 2002 there is an unconditional deterministic test (AKS), but it is much slower.
- Least prime in a progression. Linnik proved unconditionally (1944) that the least prime $\equiv a\pmod q$ is at most $q^L$ for an absolute constant $L$. GRH gives the exponent $2+\varepsilon$.
- Artin's conjecture. Hooley proved (1967) that $2$ is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes, with the predicted density, assuming the Riemann hypothesis for the Dedekind zeta functions of the fields $\mathbb Q(\zeta_k,2^{1/k})$: a GRH beyond Dirichlet $L$-functions.

blocks.title: Exceptional zeros and what is known
blocks.body:
Unconditionally, $L(s,\chi)$ has a zero-free region $\operatorname{Re}s>1-c/\log\big(q(|t|+2)\big)$, with one possible exception: a single real simple zero $\beta$ close to $1$, which can occur only for a real character $\chi$. Such a zero, if it existed, would be a [[siegel-zeros|Siegel zero]]. Siegel's theorem shows that $L(1,\chi)\gg_\varepsilon q^{-\varepsilon}$ for real primitive $\chi$, which limits how close $\beta$ can be to $1$, but the constant is ineffective: the proof cannot compute it. Through the [[class-number-formula]] this is why lower bounds for class numbers of imaginary quadratic fields, $h(-d)\gg_\varepsilon d^{1/2-\varepsilon}$, are ineffective.

GRH rules out exceptional zeros completely and would make all these results effective. Ruling them out without GRH is the Landau–Siegel problem; see [[no-siegel]] for its current status. More modest unconditional information comes from [[zero-density]] estimates, which show that zeros far from the critical line are rare on average over $\chi$.

Why is GRH hard? Every obstacle to RH applies, and the family is infinite: one needs uniformity in $q$ as well as in the height. On the evidential side, extensive computations have found all computed zeros of many $L$-functions on the line, and the analogue for $L$-functions over function fields of curves over [[finite-fields]] is a theorem, a consequence of Weil's work.

blocks.title: Reduction to primitive characters
blocks.body: Let $\chi$ modulo $q$ be induced by the primitive character $\chi^*$. Show that the zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ in the strip $0< \operatorname{Re}s<1$ are exactly those of $L(s,\chi^*)$, so GRH for primitive characters implies GRH for all characters.
blocks.solution:
By the Euler products, for $\operatorname{Re}s>1$,

$$L(s,\chi)=\prod_{p\nmid q}\big(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s}\big)^{-1}=L(s,\chi^*)\prod_{p\mid q}\big(1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s}\big),$$

since $\chi(p)=\chi^*(p)$ for $p\nmid q$ and $\chi(p)=0$ for $p\mid q$. Both sides are meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, so the identity holds everywhere.

A factor $1-\chi^*(p)p^{-s}$ vanishes only if $\chi^*(p)\ne0$ and $p^{-s}=1/\chi^*(p)$. Since $|\chi^*(p)|=1$, this forces $|p^{-s}|=p^{-\operatorname{Re}s}=1$, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}s=0$. So the finite product has no zeros in $0< \operatorname{Re}s<1$, and the zeros there of $L(s,\chi)$ and $L(s,\chi^*)$ coincide.

For instance, the principal character modulo $6$ is induced by the trivial character, and $L(s,\chi_0)=\zeta(s)(1-2^{-s})(1-3^{-s})$ acquires extra zeros at $s=2\pi ik/\log2$ and $s=2\pi ik/\log3$, all on $\operatorname{Re}s=0$.

blocks.title: From characters to progressions
blocks.body: Assume that $\psi(x,\chi)=O(\sqrt x\log^2(qx))$ for every nonprincipal $\chi$ modulo $q$, and that $\psi(x,\chi_0)=x+O(\sqrt x\log^2x)$. Deduce the GRH bound for $\psi(x;q,a)$ when $q\le x$, and explain why it carries no information when $q$ is much larger than $\sqrt x$.
blocks.solution:
By orthogonality,

$$\psi(x;q,a)-\frac x{\varphi(q)}=\frac{\psi(x,\chi_0)-x}{\varphi(q)}+\frac1{\varphi(q)}\sum_{\chi\ne\chi_0}\bar\chi(a)\psi(x,\chi).$$

Each of the at most $\varphi(q)$ terms has absolute value $O(\sqrt x\log^2(qx))$, because $|\bar\chi(a)|=1$; dividing by $\varphi(q)$, the whole right side is $O(\sqrt x\log^2(qx))$. For $q\le x$ we have $\log(qx)\le2\log x$, giving $O(\sqrt x\log^2x)$.

(The hypothesis on $\chi_0$ is RH, since $\psi(x,\chi_0)$ differs from $\psi(x)$ only by the prime powers dividing $q$, which contribute $O(\log q\log x)$.)

Why the bound is empty for large $q$: the formula says something only when the main term $x/\varphi(q)$ exceeds the error bound $C\sqrt x\log^2x$, which requires $\varphi(q)< \sqrt x/(C\log^2x)$. If $q$ is a prime near $\sqrt x$, the main term $x/(q-1)$ is about $\sqrt x$, smaller than the error bound, so the estimate does not even show that $\psi(x;q,a)>0$. In that range the trivial bound $\psi(x;q,a)\le(x/q+1)\log x$, which holds because at most $x/q+1$ integers up to $x$ lie in the class and each has $\Lambda(n)\le\log x$, is better than the GRH bound.

blocks.title: A numerical check modulo 4
blocks.body: Compute $\psi(10^6;4,1)$ and $\psi(10^6;4,3)$ and compare the errors with $\sqrt{10^6}$.
blocks.solution:
Summing $\log p$ over prime powers $p^k\le10^6$ in each class gives

$$\psi(10^6;4,1)\approx499368.8,\qquad\psi(10^6;4,3)\approx500204.6,$$

so the errors relative to $x/2=500000$ are about $-631$ and $+205$. Both are below $\sqrt x=1000$, let alone $\sqrt x\log^2x\approx1.9\cdot10^5$. Consistent with GRH for the character modulo $4$, the errors are of size $\sqrt x$ rather than something like $x^{0.9}$. (The squares of odd primes, all $\equiv1\pmod4$, push the first class up; counting primes alone, the class $3\bmod4$ is slightly ahead, the phenomenon known as Chebyshev's bias.)

blocks.title: Small non-residues
blocks.body: For primes $3\le p<10^6$, find the largest least quadratic non-residue $n(p)$ and compare it with Bach's GRH bound $2\log^2p$.
blocks.solution: Testing $n=2,3,\dots$ with Euler's criterion $n^{(p-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod p$, the largest value in this range is $n(p)=43$, attained at $p=366791$. There $2\log^2p\approx328$, so the actual non-residue is far smaller than the bound; in fact $n(p)<2\log^2p$ for every prime in the range. Heuristics and computations suggest that the largest values of $n(p)$ grow much more slowly than $\log^2p$, so the GRH bound is probably not sharp. Its value is that it is a proved polynomial bound in $\log p$, under GRH, whereas the best unconditional bound is a power of $p$.

blocks.body:
- GRH is not needed for Dirichlet's theorem or for the prime number theorem in progressions with fixed $q$; it is about the size and uniformity of the error.
- The GRH bound for $\psi(x;q,a)$ is trivial for $q$ beyond about $\sqrt x$. Statements about larger moduli, such as Elliott–Halberstam, are not consequences of GRH.
- Bombieri–Vinogradov gives GRH-quality bounds on average over $q$, never for an individual modulus.
- For a complex character, zeros are not symmetric about the real axis; the symmetry pairs zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ with zeros of $L(s,\bar\chi)$.
- Imprimitive characters have zeros on $\operatorname{Re}s=0$ coming from the finite Euler factors; they are excluded by the condition $0< \operatorname{Re}\rho<1$ and do not contradict GRH.
- "Under GRH" in a paper may refer to Dirichlet $L$-functions or to Dedekind zeta functions; check which version is assumed.

GRH extends the [[rh]] to the [[l-functions|Dirichlet L-functions]] built from [[dirichlet-characters]]. It would give primes in progressions with square-root error, while the unconditional substitutes are the [[siegel-walfisz]] theorem for small moduli and the [[bombieri-vinogradov]] theorem on average, the latter proved with the [[large-sieve]] and the key input for [[bounded-gaps]]. It excludes [[siegel-zeros]], whose unconditional status is the subject of [[no-siegel]], and through the [[class-number-formula]] it would make class number bounds effective. The weaker [[quasi-rh|quasi-Riemann hypothesis]] and [[zero-density]] estimates are partial substitutes. Its algorithmic consequences concern [[primality]] testing and [[quadratic-residues]]; the versions for [[dedekind-zeta]] and [[hecke-l]] functions drive results such as Hooley's conditional proof of Artin's conjecture on [[order-primroot|primitive roots]].

1. Show that if $\chi$ is a real character then the zeros of $L(s,\chi)$ are symmetric under $\rho\mapsto\bar\rho$, and hence under $\rho\mapsto1-\rho$.
2. Using the GRH bound for $\psi(x;q,a)$, show that for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every large $x$, each admissible class modulo $q$ contains a prime below $x$ provided $q\le x^{1/2-\varepsilon}$.
3. Find the least quadratic non-residue modulo $p$ for all primes $p<200$, and identify the primes where it is at least $5$.
4. Explain why the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture is not implied by GRH, using the size of the error term in the GRH bound.
